v: Calgary has burned, flooded, struck oil, and hosted the world. It all began where two rivers meet.
For thousands of years, the place where the Bow and Elbow rivers join was a gathering place. The Blackfoot call it Moh-kin-stiss, the elbow.
It is the land of the Blackfoot Confederacy, the Tsoo-tee-na, and the Stoney Nakoda, and home to the May-tee.
Eighteen seventy-five. The North-West Mounted Police arrive, and build a log fort where the rivers meet.
Its commander names it Fort Breez-bwah, after himself. Nobody likes it. In eighteen seventy-six, it becomes Fort Calgary, named by James Macleod after Calgary, on Scotland's Isle of Mull.
Eighteen seventy-seven. Treaty Seven is signed at Blackfoot Crossing, between the Crown and five First Nations.
Eighteen eighty-three. The Canadian Pacific Railway arrives. Calgary becomes a town the next year, and a city in eighteen ninety-four.
Eighteen eighty-six. Fire sweeps through the wooden downtown. Calgary rebuilds in stone, and becomes the Sandstone City.
Nineteen twelve. Guy Wee-dick stages the first Stampede, backed by four cattlemen known as the Big Four.
Nineteen fourteen. Dingman Number One strikes at Turner Valley, southwest of the city. Calgary goes oil crazy.
Nineteen forty-seven. After the big Leduc discovery, oil companies make Calgary their head office, and the city booms.
Nineteen sixty-eight. The Husky Tower rises one hundred and ninety-one metres over downtown. Today, we call it the Calgary Tower.
Nineteen eighty-eight. Calgary hosts the first Winter Olympics ever held in Canada, and the tower's torch burns for sixteen days.
Twenty thirteen. The Bow and Elbow rise. About seventy-five thousand people are told to leave home, the largest evacuation in the city's history. Calgarians clean up, together.
Today, more than one and a half million people call Calgary home. A city of newcomers, still growing, where two rivers meet.
